name: Vaginal steaming

lead: Vaginal steaming is a practice in which a person sits or squats over a bowl or seat of steaming water infused with herbs such as mugwort, wormwood, rosemary or basil. Spas and wellness sellers offer it as a way to 'freshen' and 'tone' the vagina and to support reproductive wellbeing, and it is often framed as a self-care ritual that helps people feel more confident in their bodies.

It entered Western headlines in 2015 after actor Gwyneth Paltrow's lifestyle site described a spa version. Researchers have analysed how the practice is portrayed online, and clinicians have published case reports of harm; no controlled trials of the claimed benefits have been published.

paras: In spas, clients sit on a special seat over herbal steam, sometimes combined with infrared heat. At home, people use a pot or bowl of hot water with dried herbs. Traditional forms of the practice exist in parts of Africa, Asia and Central America, usually tied to postpartum or women's health customs rather than to appearance.

A 2019 Canadian case report described second-degree burns in a 62-year-old woman who steamed to try to reduce prolapse. Other reported concerns include allergic reactions, irritation and infection; a 2022 Dutch case-control study examined vaginal hygiene practices as a factor in preterm birth. Medical sources such as the Cleveland Clinic state that there is no evidence of benefit.

angle.text: Promoters present the steam session as a spa-style self-care ritual that leaves the vulva and vagina feeling fresh and 'toned'. Its role in how someone looks is a claimed, mostly subjective one, tied to confidence and wellbeing.

lead: Vaginal steaming, also called V-steaming, yoni steaming or wormwood steaming, is an alternative-wellness practice in which a woman sits or squats over steam from water infused with herbs such as mugwort, rosemary, wormwood or basil.[1] Spas and sellers present it as a way to cleanse, tone or 'revitalise' the vagina and uterus, and to support fertility, sexual wellbeing and general health.[1][2]

In appearance-minded wellness culture it is positioned as feminine grooming and self-care: promoters talk about 'freshening', tightening and feeling confident in one's body, as one of several genital-modification and hygiene practices on offer in Anglo-Western countries.[2][3] Forms of herbal steam bathing exist in parts of Africa (including Mozambique and South Africa), Asia (including Indonesia and Thailand) and Central America, including among the Q'eqchi' Maya, usually within traditional reproductive-health customs.[1]

The practice reached wide Western attention in 2015, when Gwyneth Paltrow wrote on her Goop site about a Santa Monica spa treatment combining infrared heat and mugwort steam that supposedly 'cleanses your uterus'; The Guardian and other outlets responded with warnings from clinicians.[1][2] Published research consists of media and discourse analysis, qualitative interviews, observational studies and case reports rather than trials of benefit.
infobox: Reproductive and postpartum customs in parts of Africa, Asia and Central America

paras: The practitioner or user squats or sits over a bowl or seat of hot, herb-infused water so that the steam reaches the genital area.[1] Claimed benefits include hormone balancing, revitalising the uterus, improved fertility, increased sexual pleasure and 'detoxing'.[1][2]

Researchers Vandenburg and Braun, analysing 90 online items from news outlets, lifestyle sites, spas and personal blogs, argued that the discourse draws on ideas about women's bodies as needing cleansing and as existing for sexual and reproductive purposes.[2]

Wikipedia describes steaming practices among women in Mozambique and South Africa, Indonesia and Thailand, and Central America, and notes that spas often market the treatment as an ancient Chinese remedy for reproductive complaints.[1] Its spread into Western wellness culture is generally dated to 2015, when celebrity coverage drew widespread press.[1][2]

A 2026 qualitative study of eight Black women in the USA found mixed views, with participants weighing cultural meaning against perceived risk; only one had personally tried it.[4] A 2026 preprint at a Ugandan sexually-transmitted-infection clinic examined how common steaming was among attendees and compared vaginal bacterial profiles.[5]

A 2019 case report in the Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada described a 62-year-old woman who sustained second-degree burns after steaming in an attempt to reduce vaginal prolapse; the authors said clinicians should be aware of alternative treatments so counselling can reduce harm.[6] Other reported concerns include allergic reactions, burns when the steam source is too close, and vaginal or urinary infections.[1]

A 2022 Dutch case-control study of 79 women with spontaneous preterm birth and 156 with term birth investigated vaginal hygiene practices as a possible factor.[7] The Cleveland Clinic is cited as stating there is no evidence of benefit.[1]

No clinical trials of vaginal steaming for the benefits claimed have been published. Related research consists of a case report of burns,[6] observational studies of vaginal hygiene practices,[7] a clinic-based study of steaming prevalence,[5] and qualitative and media analyses of how the practice is perceived and portrayed.[2][4]
